1. Oral Cavity: Lips, Tongue and Taste Buds

Lips (three regions)

RegionEpitheliumKey features
Red marginThicker, keratinized stratified squamousNo glands (so lips dry out), deep dermal papillae (friction), highly vascular (red color)
Oral mucosa of the lipPartially keratinized near the red margin, then non-keratinized stratified squamousGlands present
Thin skin of the lipKeratinized stratified squamousHair follicles present, like skin elsewhere
Lip: red margin, oral mucosa, thin skin (click to enlarge)

Tongue

  • Stratified squamous epithelium with papillae; skeletal muscle in many orientations (the giveaway); both serous and mucous glands.
Tongue (click to enlarge)

Lingual papillae

PapillaShape / IDTaste buds?Notes
FiliformCone-shaped, sharp point; most commonNoIncrease surface area and friction to move the food bolus
FungiformMushroom-shaped; scattered among filiformYes, apicalTaste buds may not appear in the section
CircumvallateLargest; big troughsYes, lining the troughsLingual salivary glands at the base of the invaginations flush the troughs
FoliateBlock-like, curved with troughs between; usually three cores of lamina propriaYes, lateral
Filiform and fungiform papillae (click to enlarge)
Circumvallate papilla (click to enlarge)

Taste bud

Oval, pale-staining, with an apical pore. Present in foliate, fungiform and circumvallate papillae (not filiform).

Foliate papilla and taste bud (click to enlarge)
CellPosition / stainFunction
BasalAt the base; does not span the budStem cell (high turnover) that gives rise to the other two
SupportingSpans the full length; darker stainingPhysical and metabolic support of sensory cells
SensorySpans the full length; lighter staining, often centralDetects taste; microvilli at the pore increase surface area
Taste bud cells (click to enlarge)

2. Salivary Glands

Organization (any gland)

StructureID
LobeLarge division, separated by interlobar connective tissue (CT) containing vessels and ducts
LobuleSmaller division, separated by interlobular CT containing vessels and ducts
Lobe and lobule of a salivary gland (click to enlarge)

Duct system (smallest → largest)

DuctEpitheliumID
IntercalatedSimple cuboidalTiny lumen; about the size of the acini; feeds into striated duct
StriatedSimple columnar (or cuboidal)Basal striations (mitochondria); sits within the parenchyma, with little CT; feeds into the excretory duct
ExcretorySimple or stratified cuboidal, or stratified columnar (varies with size)Largest duct; always surrounded by CT (interlobular/interlobar); connects the gland to the oral cavity
Intercalated, striated and excretory ducts (click to enlarge)

The three major glands

GlandSecretionID
ParotidAlmost entirely serousLargest; often adipose cells present
SubmandibularMostly serous with some mucousMostly dark serous acini plus mixed acini
SublingualMostly mucousPale, hazy mucinous acini dominate
AcinusLook
SerousDark (eosinophilic and basophilic granules); round nuclei near the periphery
MucinousPale, hazy; flattened nuclei pushed to the edge
MixedPale mucous cells in the center with darker serous cells at the edge
Parotid gland: serous acini (click to enlarge)
Submandibular gland: mixed acini (click to enlarge)
Sublingual gland: mucinous acini (click to enlarge)

3. Layers of the GI Tract

LayerSublayers / contents
1. Mucosa (most apical)Three sublayers: epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae
2. SubmucosaDense irregular CT, no sublayers; vessels; submucosal plexus; glands in some regions (esophagus, duodenum)
3. Muscularis externaTwo smooth muscle sublayers; contains the myenteric plexus
4. Serosa / adventitiaOutermost. Adventitia: one sublayer (CT), attaches to adjoining structures. Serosa: two sublayers (CT + mesothelium), free in the abdominal cavity
The four layers of the GI tract (click to enlarge)

Sublayers

SublayerFeatures
EpitheliumSimple columnar in most regions (esophagus is the exception); absorption and secretion
Lamina propriaLoose CT, vessels, lymphatics, diffuse lymphatic tissue
Muscularis mucosaeThin smooth muscle; helps gland secretion; may be incomplete
Circular layerSmooth muscle, always the more superficial of the two; compresses and mixes chyme
Longitudinal layerSmooth muscle, always deeper; shortens to move chyme along. Circular + longitudinal together produce peristalsis
Connective tissueLoose and dense irregular CT of serosa and adventitia
MesotheliumSimple squamous; serosa only; secretes serous fluid, reduces friction
The seven sublayers (click to enlarge)

Enteric plexuses

PlexusLocationID
Myenteric (Auerbach)Between circular and longitudinal layers of the muscularis externaNeuron cell bodies with satellite cells; larger
Submucosal (Meissner)In the submucosaLighter staining, smaller, harder to find
Myenteric and submucosal plexuses (click to enlarge)
Not shown on the slides (in red on his list)Enteroendocrine cells need special stains and are left to the first-year quizzes.

4. Esophagus and Stomach

Esophagus

  • Stratified squamous epithelium (unique among GI regions); skeletal muscle proximally transitioning to smooth muscle distally; upper and lower esophageal sphincters (thickened muscularis externa).
  • Esophageal glands: mucus-secreting, in the submucosa; lubricate and hold the bolus together.
Esophagus and esophageal glands (click to enlarge)

Esophagogastric (gastroesophageal) junction

Abrupt change from stratified squamous (esophagus) to simple columnar (cardia of the stomach), mostly mucous cells.

Esophagogastric junction (click to enlarge)

Stomach (fundus)

  • Gastric pits (shallow) lined by surface mucous cells; gastric glands (deep, down to the muscularis mucosae).
  • Gastric glands contain: parietal (pink), chief (purple), stem cells, mucous neck cells, and enteroendocrine cells.
Gastric pits and glands (click to enlarge)
CellIDProduct
ChiefDeeper in the gland; basophilic at the base, eosinophilic apicallyPepsinogen
ParietalEosinophilic (pink); outnumber chief cells in the upper/mid glandHCl and intrinsic factor (vitamin B12 absorption)
Surface mucousHazy, most superficial; line the pitsThick mucus with bicarbonate (protects from acid)
Chief, parietal and surface mucous cells (click to enlarge)

5. Small Intestine

Shared structures

StructureID / function
VilliFinger-like projections of epithelium + lamina propria; contain blood vessels and a lacteal; ↑ surface area
LactealBlind-ended lymphatic capillary in the center of the villus (empty-looking space); transports large molecules such as chylomicrons
Intestinal glands (crypts)Simple tubular glands between villi extending to the muscularis mucosae; contain goblet cells, enterocytes, M cells, enteroendocrine cells, Paneth cells
EnterocyteMost common cell; dark microvilli (brush border); absorption
Goblet cellHazy, goblet-shaped; produces mucus
Paneth cellBright eosinophilic granules at the base of the crypts; innate immunity (antimicrobial peptides, lysozyme)
Plicae circularesLarge folds of mucosa + submucosa only (no muscularis externa); most prominent in the jejunum
Small intestine structures and cells (click to enlarge)

Regions

RegionID
Duodenum (first ~6 in.)Villi + duodenal glands in the submucosa (secrete alkaline fluid to neutralize stomach acid; also called Brunner glands). Liver, gallbladder and pancreatic secretions enter here; heavy chemical digestion
Jejunum"Vanilla": villi but no submucosal glands and no Peyer patches; greatest absorption; prominent plicae circulares
IleumPeyer patches (lymphatic nodules, dark basophilic lymphocytes, in lamina propria down into submucosa); absorption and immune surveillance
Duodenum with duodenal glands (click to enlarge)
Jejunum with plicae circulares (click to enlarge)
Ileum with Peyer patches (click to enlarge)

6. Large Intestine, Appendix and Rectoanal Junction

RegionID
ColonFlat mucosa (no villi, no plicae circulares); very many goblet cells; also columnar absorptive cells, M cells, enteroendocrine cells; water and electrolyte absorption. No gastric-type pits or glands
Teniae coliThickened longitudinal muscle bands (three) of the muscularis externa; help move material along
AppendixWorm-like appendage of the cecum; flat mucosa like colon but many lymphatic nodules (like Peyer patches); no villi
Rectoanal junctionSimple columnar (rectum) → intermediate epithelium → keratinized stratified squamous (anus); internal and external anal sphincters (thickened muscularis externa)
Colon (click to enlarge)
Teniae coli (click to enlarge)
Appendix (click to enlarge)
Rectoanal junction (click to enlarge)

7. Liver, Gallbladder and Pancreas

Liver

  • Hepatic lobule = basic unit: one central vein (terminal hepatic venule) with sinusoids radiating to it; portal triads (usually 4–6) at the corners.
Liver: lobule, central vein, portal triad (click to enlarge)
Portal triad componentID / function
Portal veinLargest vessel; nutrient-rich, deoxygenated blood from the intestines; delivers the majority of liver blood
Hepatic arteryThick wall with elastic fibers; oxygenated blood; about ¼ of liver blood
Bile ductSimple cuboidal or columnar epithelium; collects bile from hepatocytes
Periportal space (space of Mall)Empty-looking space with blind-ended lymphatic capillaries
  • Sinusoids: capillaries (white spaces) carrying portal and arterial blood past hepatocytes to the central vein.
  • Hepatocytes: eosinophilic cuboidal cells in single file along the sinusoids; detoxify, lipid metabolism, make bile.
Portal triad and hepatocytes (click to enlarge)
Not shown on the slides (in red on his list)Kupffer cells (macrophages in the sinusoids; need a special stain) and the perisinusoidal space (space of Disse; seen only by electron microscopy, between hepatocytes and sinusoid; hepatocyte microvilli aid exchange).

Gallbladder

  • Simple columnar epithelium (cholangiocytes, which modify bile); no submucosa and no muscularis mucosae (lamina propria goes straight into a thick, somewhat disorganized muscularis externa); stores bile and removes water.
  • Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses: epithelial invaginations that can reach into the muscularis externa.
Gallbladder and Rokitansky-Aschoff sinus (click to enlarge)

Pancreas

  • Acinar cells (bright pink/purple, exocrine enzymes) with pale islets of Langerhans (alpha, beta, delta cells; hormones).
Pancreas: acini and islet (click to enlarge)

8. Quick Identification Table

If you see…It's…
Stratified squamous + skeletal muscle in all orientations + serous and mucous glandsTongue
Keratinized stratified squamous, no glands, deep papillaeRed margin of lip
Cone-shaped papillae, no taste budsFiliform
Huge papillae with troughs and gland ducts at the baseCircumvallate
Basal striations on a columnar duct inside the aciniStriated duct
Mostly dark serous acini + adiposeParotid
Pale mucinous acini with flat peripheral nuclei dominateSublingual
Stratified squamous mucosa + submucosal mucous glandsEsophagus
Pits + deep glands with pink and purple cellsStomach (fundus)
Villi + submucosal glandsDuodenum
Villi, no submucosal glands, no Peyer patchesJejunum
Villi + Peyer patchesIleum
Flat mucosa + many goblet cellsColon
Flat mucosa + many lymphatic nodulesAppendix
Simple columnar → keratinized stratified squamousRectoanal junction
Central vein with radiating sinusoids; triads at the edgeLiver
Simple columnar, no submucosa, thick disorganized muscleGallbladder
Pink acini with pale islandsPancreas
